chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Asimi, from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Taymuli, from Amr ibn Uthman, from Abu Jameela, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
A man from the people of Khurasan in al-Rabadhah said to him: 'May I be your ransom, I have not been granted a child.'
So he said to him: 'When you return to your land and intend to go to your wife, so recite when you intend that.'

The one with the whale (Yunus), when he went away in anger, so he thought that We had no Power over him, so he called out in the darkness: There is no god but You, Glory be to You; surely I am from the unjust ones.
Up to three verses, so you will be granted a child, God willing.

key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a phrase of respect)
key_terms.ذَا النُّونِ: The one with the whale (referring to Prophet Yunus)

ai.seo_question: What is the recommended supplication for having children in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, the Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) prescribes the recitation of the verses of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) from Surah Al-Anbiya as a specific means to secure offspring, linking the supplicant's intent with the divine promise of relief from distress. This practice highlights the Shia emphasis on the intercessory power of Quranic verses and the spiritual efficacy of invoking the experience of the Prophets to overcome personal barrenness. The instruction to recite 'until three verses' underscores the precision required in this devotional act, reflecting the broader theological view that divine mercy is accessible through specific, prophetic patterns of worship.
